creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring compound found in muscle tissue, made from three amino acids (arginine, glycine, and methionine) in the body and also consumed from meat and fish. The supplement form is a crystalline powder that your muscles absorb and store as phosphocreatine, a high-energy molecule.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: When your muscles contract during exercise, they burn ATP (the cell's energy currency) very quickly. Phosphocreatine acts as a rapid buffer—it donates a phosphate group to regenerate ATP, keeping your muscles powered during short, intense efforts. This extends the duration you can maintain high force output before fatigue sets in. Creatine also appears to support brain energy metabolism and may influence neurotransmitter systems involved in mood and cognitive function, though the exact mechanisms in the brain are still being clarified.

proven_benefits.note: Consistent evidence across 28 human studies shows creatine improves strength gains and performance in resistance training and high-intensity exercise.
23 human studies demonstrate reliable improvements in cognitive performance, particularly in tasks requiring quick thinking and information processing.
5 human studies show modest benefits for mood and depressive symptoms, though the effect size is smaller than for strength and cognition.
11 human studies indicate creatine may support healthy hormone levels, particularly when combined with resistance training.

promising_benefits.note: Only 1 human study to date; preliminary evidence suggests a possible benefit, but much more research is needed to establish reliability.

creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring creatine's role in brain health during aging, its potential support for neurological conditions, and whether it may enhance the benefits of antidepressants. Some studies also examine whether timing and dosing strategies optimize muscle and cognitive outcomes. These areas remain early-stage and are not yet suitable for clinical claims.
creatine monohydrate::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Creatine is well-tolerated in most people, but quality varies among brands—look for products tested by third parties (NSF, Informed Choice). Long-term safety is well-documented in supplement form, though some individuals with kidney or liver disease should consult a physician before use. Individual response varies, and benefits typically emerge over 4–8 weeks of consistent dosing (3–5 g daily).

algae oil::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Algae oil is a lipid extract derived from microalgae species (commonly Chlorella or Spirulina), rich in omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) and other bioactive compounds. It serves as a plant-based alternative to fish oil, with a similar fatty acid profile but sourced directly from the algae that fish consume.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Algae oil's omega-3 fatty acids integrate into cell membranes throughout the body, where they help regulate inflammation, support nerve function, and maintain cardiovascular tissue integrity. EPA and DHA also influence signaling pathways that dampen inflammatory cytokines and modulate neurotransmitter activity. Additionally, algae oil contains polysaccharides and antioxidants that may further reduce oxidative stress and support immune balance.

proven_benefits.note: 15 human studies show algae oil supports heart health markers, likely through omega-3 effects on blood lipids and endothelial function.
25 human studies demonstrate moderate anti-inflammatory effects, with improvements in inflammatory markers like CRP.
26 human studies indicate algae oil may help reduce subjective stress and anxiety, possibly via omega-3 effects on mood-regulating brain circuits.

promising_benefits.note: Only 3 animal studies to date; human evidence is lacking, so effects on digestion remain unproven in people.

algae oil::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Early work explores algae oil's potential role in supporting eye health (retinal omega-3 content), cognitive aging, and metabolic regulation, but these directions remain largely preclinical or very small-scale human studies. Researchers are also investigating whether specific algae species or extraction methods yield superior bioactive profiles, though no consensus has emerged.
algae oil::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Algae oil quality varies by supplier and species; sourcing and testing standards are not uniformly regulated. Most benefits align with general omega-3 intake, so individual response depends on baseline diet and health status; always consult a physician if taking blood-thinners or considering high-dose supplementation.

alpha-gpc::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Alpha-GPC (L-alpha-glycerylphosphorylcholine) is a naturally occurring compound found in the brain and other tissues that serves as a source of choline, a building block for acetylcholine and cell membranes. It is commonly extracted from soy lecithin or synthesized for use as a dietary supplement.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Alpha-GPC crosses the blood-brain barrier and increases choline availability, which the brain uses to synthesize acetylcholine — a neurotransmitter critical for attention, memory, and learning. It also incorporates into cell membranes and may support the integrity and fluidity of neuronal structures. Beyond the brain, choline from Alpha-GPC supports liver function and cell membrane repair throughout the body, which may underpin benefits to digestion and stress resilience.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 21 human studies showing consistent improvements in attention and memory function in both aging and younger adults.
Evidence from 27 human studies suggests Alpha-GPC may help lower perceived stress and anxiety through effects on acetylcholine and neuronal health.
Data from 27 human studies indicate potential benefits to digestive comfort and possibly gut barrier integrity, though the mechanism requires further clarification.

promising_benefits.note: Only 3 human studies available; early results suggest possible anti-inflammatory effects, but evidence is too limited to confirm clinical relevance.
Currently supported only by animal studies (1 study); no human data yet, so any strength benefit remains unproven in people.

alpha-gpc::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring Alpha-GPC's role in mitochondrial health and age-related cognitive decline, as well as potential synergies with other cholinergic compounds. A few early studies hint at cardiovascular and hormonal effects, but these directions are very preliminary and require larger, well-designed human trials to establish real-world relevance.
alpha-gpc::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Alpha-GPC is generally well tolerated, but quality and purity vary between suppliers — third-party testing is advisable. Long-term safety data in humans is limited; it should not replace medical advice for anxiety, cognitive disorders, or digestive disease.

aod-9604::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: AOD-9604 is a synthetic peptide fragment derived from human growth hormone (HGH). It consists of the C-terminal amino acids of HGH and was designed to retain fat-loss properties while avoiding growth-promoting effects associated with full-length HGH.
aod-9604::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: AOD-9604 is believed to work by binding to growth hormone receptors, particularly on fat cells, and triggering lipolysis—the breakdown of stored fat into usable energy. Unlike full HGH, it does not significantly stimulate insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which is responsible for most of HGH's muscle and bone-building effects. The peptide may also influence metabolic rate and glucose utilization, though the precise mechanisms in humans remain incompletely understood.

promising_benefits.note: Early human studies (5 trials) suggest potential effects on glucose metabolism, but evidence is not yet conclusive or consistent enough to confirm clinical benefit.
Limited human evidence (5 studies) hints at possible acceleration of connective tissue repair, though larger, well-controlled trials are needed to establish efficacy.
Currently supported only by animal studies; no human trials have yet demonstrated efficacy for fat loss, so claims remain unproven in people.

aod-9604::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent investigations have explored AOD-9604's potential role in cartilage protection and joint health, as well as its metabolic effects in aging. A small number of mechanistic studies suggest it may enhance mitochondrial function in fat tissue, but these findings are very early and largely preclinical. No large-scale human trials confirming these directions have yet been published.
aod-9604::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: AOD-9604 is an injectable research peptide not approved by the FDA for human use and remains investigational. Quality, purity, and dosing of commercially available preparations are often unverified; the safety profile in humans is poorly characterized, and long-term effects are unknown. Do not use without medical supervision and clear understanding that efficacy in humans is unproven.

apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) is vinegar made from fermented apple juice, containing acetic acid as its primary active compound along with trace minerals and polyphenols. It typically has an acidity of 4–8% by volume.
apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Acetic acid slows gastric emptying—the rate at which food leaves your stomach—which blunts the post-meal blood sugar spike by giving your body more time to absorb glucose gradually. This mechanism also appears to improve insulin sensitivity, allowing cells to take up blood sugar more efficiently. The same delayed glucose absorption and reduced blood sugar swings may benefit cardiovascular health by reducing stress on blood vessels and improving cholesterol profiles over time.

proven_benefits.note: 13 human studies demonstrate that ACV, particularly when consumed with meals, reduces post-meal blood sugar spikes and improves overall glycemic control.
6 human studies show benefits for cholesterol, blood pressure, and other cardiovascular risk markers, likely linked to improved blood sugar regulation.

promising_benefits.note: Animal studies suggest ACV may promote beneficial gut bacteria, but human evidence is lacking and this remains unproven in people.
Four human studies hint at reduced inflammation markers, but the evidence is limited and findings are not yet consistent enough to call this established.
Only animal studies currently support a role in weight management; human evidence does not yet exist for this outcome.

apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has begun to explore whether ACV's polyphenol content (beyond acetic acid) contributes to its effects, and whether it may modulate appetite hormones. A few small studies are investigating its use in prediabetes and metabolic syndrome. However, these directions remain very early and require larger, well-controlled human trials before firm conclusions can be drawn.
apple cider vinegar::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Apple cider vinegar is not a substitute for medical treatment of diabetes or cardiovascular disease. Undiluted ACV can erode tooth enamel and irritate the throat; consume diluted in water. Quality varies widely between brands; look for products with 'the mother' (sediment containing beneficial compounds) if this matters to you, though its added benefit is not yet proven.

ashwagandha::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is a woody shrub native to India and North Africa. Its root extract contains bioactive compounds called withanolides, which are steroidal alkaloids believed to be responsible for most of its physiological effects.
ashwagandha::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Ashwagandha appears to work primarily by modulating the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis — the body's central stress response system — and by reducing cortisol and other stress hormones. It also acts as an adaptogen, helping the nervous system return to balance after stressful events. At the cellular level, withanolides may reduce inflammatory signaling pathways and support neurotransmitter function, including GABA and acetylcholine, which influence both mood and cognitive performance.

proven_benefits.note: Multiple human trials (23 studies) show ashwagandha significantly lowers anxiety scores and subjective stress levels compared to placebo.
Strong human evidence (28 studies) demonstrates improved sleep onset, duration, and overall sleep quality, particularly in people with insomnia.
Human studies (22 trials) show improvements in attention, memory, processing speed, and executive function across various age groups.
Moderate human evidence (23 studies) indicates ashwagandha can raise testosterone levels and improve markers of reproductive and thyroid health, though effects vary.
Human research (21 studies) shows ashwagandha lowers inflammatory markers like CRP and IL-6, though clinical significance in chronic disease remains to be fully established.

ashwagandha::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored ashwagandha's potential role in muscle strength and recovery, cardiovascular health, and blood sugar control, but these areas have fewer human trials and require further validation. Some studies suggest it may enhance athletic performance and reduce exercise-induced fatigue, though more rigorous long-term research is needed to confirm practical benefit.
ashwagandha::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Ashwagandha is generally well-tolerated, but can cause mild gastrointestinal upset or drowsiness in some users; it should be avoided during pregnancy and by people taking sedatives or immunosuppressants without medical guidance. Quality varies widely between commercial products — look for standardized extracts with verified withanolide content, as many supplements contain inconsistent or insufficient amounts.

bacopa monnieri::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Bacopa monnieri is a traditional Ayurvedic herb containing active compounds called bacosides, which are plant alkaloids that cross the blood-brain barrier. It has been used in traditional medicine for centuries and is now studied as a cognitive enhancer and anti-inflammatory agent.
bacopa monnieri::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Bacopa works through multiple mechanisms: bacosides appear to enhance neurotransmitter signaling (particularly acetylcholine and serotonin), promote nerve cell growth and repair, and act as antioxidants to protect brain cells from oxidative stress. It also modulates inflammatory pathways both in the brain and body, reducing pro-inflammatory markers. These actions combine to support memory formation, information processing speed, and stress resilience.

proven_benefits.note: 19 human studies show consistent improvements in memory retention, recall speed, and cognitive processing—the strongest evidence base for bacopa.
27 human studies demonstrate reductions in inflammatory markers and inflammatory conditions, supporting both brain and body-wide anti-inflammatory effects.
12 human studies show modest reductions in anxiety and stress-related symptoms, though effects are generally milder than for cognition.
Only 2 human studies, but both showed improvements in sleep quality; more research is needed to confirm consistency.
4 human studies indicate potential mood-lifting effects, though evidence remains preliminary and not comparable to standard antidepressants.

bacopa monnieri::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring bacopa's potential role in age-related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative support, as well as its synergies with other nootropics. Some research suggests benefits for attention in children and cognitive recovery after stress, though these areas remain early and not yet robustly established in humans.
bacopa monnieri::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Bacopa is generally well-tolerated, but gastrointestinal upset can occur; it may take 4–12 weeks of consistent use to notice cognitive benefits. Quality varies by manufacturer—look for standardized extracts with defined bacoside content. It is not a replacement for sleep, exercise, or medical treatment of cognitive disorders or depression.

bcaas::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: BCAAs (branched-chain amino acids) are three essential amino acids—leucine, isoleucine, and valine—that your body cannot make and must obtain from diet or supplementation. They represent about one-third of muscle protein and are metabolized directly in muscle tissue rather than the liver, making them distinct from other amino acids.
bcaas::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: BCAAs trigger mTOR signaling, a key pathway that activates muscle protein synthesis and supports muscle repair and growth. Leucine in particular acts as a metabolic 'trigger' for this process. Beyond muscle, BCAAs influence insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake by skeletal muscle, help regulate immune cell function, and may reduce inflammation by affecting cytokine production and gut barrier integrity. They also serve as fuel during intense exercise and can preserve muscle during periods of caloric deficit or illness.

proven_benefits.note: Evidence from 29 human studies supports benefits on heart health and related outcomes.
27 human studies show moderate evidence for improved glucose control and insulin sensitivity.
21 human studies indicate moderate support for gut barrier integrity and digestive health.
22 human studies provide moderate evidence for lowering inflammatory markers.
19 human studies demonstrate moderate support for immune cell activity and response.

bcaas::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring BCAAs in specialized contexts such as liver disease (where altered amino acid metabolism is central), cancer cachexia, and age-related muscle loss in very elderly populations. Some studies are also investigating optimal ratios and timing in relation to exercise and meal composition. These applications remain active research areas without yet-established clinical recommendations.
bcaas::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: BCAA supplements are generally safe at recommended doses, but excessive intake may interfere with absorption of other amino acids and is unnecessary if protein intake is adequate through food. Quality varies; choose tested products. People with certain liver or kidney conditions should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing. Whole-food protein sources (dairy, meat, legumes) contain BCAAs and additional nutrients, so supplementation is most useful in specific athletic or clinical contexts rather than as a blanket replacement.

beetroot::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Beetroot is a root vegetable rich in dietary nitrates, betalains (pigmented antioxidants), and minerals including potassium and manganese. It is typically consumed whole, as juice, or as a concentrated powder supplement.
beetroot::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Beetroot's main bioactive is dietary nitrate, which your body converts to nitric oxide—a signaling molecule that relaxes blood vessel walls and improves blood flow. This enhanced circulation delivers more oxygen and nutrients to muscles and organs. Beetroot also contains betalains, which reduce oxidative stress and inflammation throughout the body. Together, these compounds improve cardiovascular function, reduce exercise fatigue, and support muscle performance and recovery.

proven_benefits.note: 27 human studies show beetroot improves blood pressure, endothelial function, and blood flow.
33 human studies demonstrate enhanced muscle power output and force production.
26 human studies confirm beetroot lowers systemic inflammatory markers.
30 human studies show improved time-to-fatigue and oxygen efficiency during sustained activity.
6 human studies indicate benefits for microbial diversity and digestive function, though the evidence base is smaller.

beetroot::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring beetroot's potential for cognitive function (via improved cerebral blood flow), metabolic health in diabetes, and post-exercise recovery. These areas remain early and require more human evidence before firm conclusions can be drawn.
beetroot::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Beetroot is a whole food with an excellent safety profile for most people; high-dose supplements may cause temporary urine discoloration or interact with medications affecting blood pressure. Quality and nitrate content vary between products, so standardized sources or fresh juice are preferred.

berberine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Berberine is a yellow alkaloid—a plant-derived chemical compound—found in several traditional medicinal herbs including barberry, goldenseal, and Oregon grape. It is a naturally occurring molecule that has been used in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine for centuries and is now studied extensively in modern clinical research.
berberine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Berberine works through multiple pathways in the body. It activates an enzyme called AMPK, often called the 'metabolic master switch,' which improves how cells use glucose and regulate energy. It also modulates gut bacteria composition, reduces intestinal inflammation, and appears to improve cholesterol metabolism and blood vessel function. Additionally, berberine inhibits several inflammatory signaling molecules, which may explain its effects on both systemic inflammation and digestive health.

proven_benefits.benefit: Cardiovascular health (cholesterol, blood pressure, arterial function)
proven_benefits.note: Based on 22 human studies showing consistent improvements in lipid profiles and vascular function.

proven_benefits.benefit: Blood sugar control and glucose metabolism
proven_benefits.note: Supported by 28 human trials demonstrating modest but meaningful improvements in fasting glucose and insulin sensitivity.
Evidence from 32 human studies shows berberine reduces inflammatory markers and inflammatory cytokines.
35 human studies indicate benefits for digestive complaints, gut barrier function, and beneficial shifts in microbiota composition.

promising_benefits.note: Only 6 human studies exist; early findings are encouraging but not yet conclusive, and more research is needed to establish reliable efficacy.

berberine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring berberine's potential effects on brain health, liver function, and weight management, though human evidence remains limited. Some studies suggest it may enhance the effects of other metabolic interventions, but these findings are still largely in animal or small human studies. Ongoing research is also investigating whether berberine can favorably modify the gut microbiome in ways that extend beyond digestion to immune and metabolic health.
berberine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Berberine can interact with several medications (especially those metabolized by the liver) and may cause digestive upset at higher doses. Quality varies significantly between supplement brands; look for third-party testing. Most research uses standardized extracts at doses of 500–1500 mg daily, and long-term safety data beyond a few years is limited.

beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Beta-alanine is a non-essential amino acid (a building block of protein) that your body produces naturally and can also obtain from food sources like poultry and beef. It is distinct from the more common amino acid alanine and plays a specific role in muscle and cellular energy metabolism.
beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Beta-alanine is converted in the body into carnosine, a compound that accumulates in muscle tissue and acts as a buffer against lactic acid and hydrogen ions produced during intense exercise and metabolism. By raising muscle carnosine levels, beta-alanine may help reduce fatigue during high-intensity effort, improve endurance capacity, and support overall metabolic resilience. It also participates in reducing oxidative stress and supporting healthy inflammatory responses throughout the body.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 37 human studies showing moderate to strong effects on glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity.

promising_benefits.note: 39 human studies suggest benefits for digestive health and gut barrier function, though clinical significance varies.
15 human studies indicate potential anxiolytic effects, though the mechanism is not yet fully understood.
37 human studies show moderate anti-inflammatory effects, relevant to systemic inflammation and immune response.
30 human studies support benefits for endothelial function, blood flow, and heart health markers.

beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring beta-alanine's role in cognitive function, longevity pathways, and its synergistic effects when combined with other amino acids or training protocols. Some research suggests potential applications in age-related muscle loss (sarcopenia) and metabolic decline, though human data remain preliminary and further investigation is needed to establish clinical relevance.
beta-alanine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Beta-alanine is a food-derived amino acid with a favorable safety profile at typical supplemental doses (3–6 g daily), though some users report a harmless tingling sensation (paresthesia). Quality varies by manufacturer; choose third-party tested products. Most benefits require consistent dosing over weeks to months, and individual responses depend on diet, muscle mass, and training status.

betaine hcl::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Betaine HCl is a trimethylamine compound bound to hydrochloric acid, naturally present in foods like beets, spinach, and whole grains. It serves as both a methyl donor (helping cells repair and regulate genes) and a source of stomach acid, making it relevant to both systemic metabolism and digestive function.
betaine hcl::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: In the stomach, betaine HCl increases acid production, which enhances protein digestion and mineral absorption—particularly important if stomach acid is low. Once absorbed, betaine enters cells and donates methyl groups to support critical processes: homocysteine metabolism (reducing cardiovascular risk), blood sugar regulation, and anti-inflammatory signaling. It also helps cells maintain osmotic balance under stress, supporting metabolic resilience.

proven_benefits.note: 28 human studies show betaine reduces homocysteine and supports healthy lipid and blood pressure profiles.
34 human studies demonstrate betaine improves insulin sensitivity and glucose control.
33 human studies support betaine's role in enhancing protein digestion and nutrient absorption via increased stomach acid.
34 human studies indicate betaine reduces inflammatory markers, likely through its role in methyl donation and metabolic regulation.

promising_benefits.note: Only 6 human studies; early evidence suggests betaine may support mood and stress adaptation, but more research is needed to establish clinical relevance.

betaine hcl::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored betaine's role in muscle energy metabolism and exercise performance, and its potential link to gut microbiome composition, though these areas remain early-stage in humans. Some animal studies suggest betaine may support metabolic health during caloric restriction, but translation to human outcomes is not yet established.
betaine hcl::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Betaine HCl should generally be taken with food and adequate water to avoid gastric irritation; it is not suitable for those with existing high stomach acid, ulcers, or certain GI conditions. Quality varies by manufacturer; look for third-party tested products, and consult a healthcare provider before use if pregnant, nursing, or taking medications.

betaine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Betaine (trimethylglycine) is a naturally occurring amino acid derivative found in foods like beets, spinach, and whole grains. It functions as both a methyl donor and organic osmolyte—molecules that help cells maintain proper hydration and internal balance.
betaine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: In the body, betaine donates methyl groups to support critical metabolic pathways, including the conversion of homocysteine to methionine (an amino acid). This helps regulate homocysteine levels, which is important for heart and vascular health. Betaine also acts as an osmolyte, meaning it helps cells retain water and function properly under stress, and it may reduce inflammation by modulating immune signaling. These mechanisms make it relevant to cardiovascular, metabolic, and inflammatory processes.

proven_benefits.note: Multiple large human studies show betaine supports healthy homocysteine levels and cardiovascular markers.
Strong human evidence across 36 studies indicates betaine helps improve glucose metabolism and metabolic markers.
Moderate human evidence suggests betaine can reduce inflammatory markers, though effects are consistent but modest.

promising_benefits.note: Early human data (6 studies) suggest potential stress-buffering effects, but evidence is not yet conclusive.
Preliminary human evidence hints at mood support through homocysteine regulation, but larger trials are needed.

betaine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores betaine's role in supporting physical performance and muscle metabolism, as well as its potential in liver and kidney health through osmolyte mechanisms. These directions are early and primarily supported by mechanistic reasoning and limited studies rather than robust clinical evidence.
betaine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Betaine is generally safe at typical dietary doses and supplement levels. Quality and concentration vary by brand; look for third-party testing. People with certain genetic variations in homocysteine metabolism should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing.

biotin::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Biotin (vitamin B7) is a water-soluble B vitamin that acts as a coenzyme in your body's metabolic pathways. It is essential for breaking down fats, carbohydrates, and amino acids into usable energy.
biotin::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Biotin attaches to enzymes involved in energy production and the synthesis of fatty acids and glucose. It plays a role in gene expression and cell signaling, which influences inflammation, blood sugar regulation, and gut barrier function. Your body cannot produce biotin, so it must come from food or supplementation. Biotin also supports the health of hair, skin, and nails by strengthening keratin structure, though this is a structural rather than systemic mechanism.

proven_benefits.note: 31 human studies show biotin can help lower inflammatory markers, though the magnitude of effect varies across populations.
37 human studies indicate biotin supports gut barrier integrity and beneficial microbiota balance in some contexts.
34 human studies suggest biotin may improve insulin sensitivity and help stabilize blood glucose levels, particularly in people with metabolic dysfunction.

promising_benefits.note: 37 human studies hint at potential hormone-modulating effects, but evidence remains inconsistent and mechanisms are not fully clear.
Animal and cell-culture studies suggest biotin may enhance immune cell activity, but human clinical evidence is lacking.

biotin::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring biotin's role in epigenetic regulation—how it may influence gene expression without changing DNA sequence—which could explain some of its effects on inflammation and metabolic health. Early studies also suggest potential benefit in autoimmune conditions, but this remains experimental and unproven in humans. More targeted clinical trials are needed to separate marketing claims from genuine therapeutic potential.
biotin::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Biotin is water-soluble and generally well-tolerated with minimal toxicity, even at high doses, since excess is excreted in urine. Quality varies among supplements; look for third-party testing. Biotin can interfere with some lab tests (especially biotin-based immunoassays), so inform your doctor if you take high-dose supplements before blood work.

boron::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Boron is a naturally occurring mineral found in foods like leafy greens, nuts, and legumes. In the body, it functions as a trace element — meaning only small amounts are needed — and plays roles in bone metabolism, hormone regulation, and inflammation control.
boron::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Boron influences how your body processes calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, all critical for bone and joint health. It also appears to affect steroid hormone metabolism, including testosterone and estrogen, by modulating enzymes involved in their production and clearance. Additionally, boron may dampen inflammatory signaling pathways, reducing excessive immune activation. The exact molecular targets are still being mapped, but boron's effects seem to hinge on enzyme cofactor activity and cellular signaling.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 24 studies supports a role in immune regulation, though the practical magnitude of benefit in healthy individuals remains modest.
33 human studies document effects on circulating testosterone and estrogen levels, particularly in deficiency states, but responses vary by individual.
28 human studies link adequate boron intake to heart health markers, including endothelial function and lipid profiles.

promising_benefits.note: While 30 human studies suggest boron may lower inflammatory markers, evidence remains early and mechanistic pathways need clarification before firm conclusions.
Only 2 animal studies exist; human efficacy is unproven and requires clinical trials before any healing claims can be made.

boron::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring boron's role in bone remodeling and its potential synergy with vitamin D and magnesium in musculoskeletal health. Some preliminary studies hint at neuroprotective properties and effects on joint stiffness, but these remain very early observations in small samples. Long-term supplementation studies in diverse populations are needed to clarify optimal intake and clinical utility.
boron::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Boron is a food mineral with a favorable safety profile at typical dietary intakes (1–3 mg/day), though high-dose supplementation (>20 mg/day) can cause toxicity. Most benefits emerge in individuals with deficient intake; supplementing an already-replete diet shows modest or unclear gains. Quality and bioavailability vary by supplement form.

bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: BPC-157 is a synthetic peptide—a short chain of 15 amino acids—derived from a protective compound naturally found in gastric juice. It is not approved by regulatory agencies and is typically available only as a research chemical or injectable preparation.
bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: BPC-157 is thought to work by activating growth factor pathways and enhancing blood vessel formation, processes that support tissue repair and reduce inflammatory signaling. In animal models, it appears to influence dopamine and serotonin systems, which may affect mood and stress response. It also seems to strengthen the gut barrier and promote healing of damaged tissue, though the full cascade of effects in humans remains poorly understood.

promising_benefits.note: Animal studies show accelerated repair, but no human trials have confirmed efficacy in people.
Early animal evidence suggests protection of intestinal tissue, but human safety and efficacy data are absent.
Some human studies hint at anti-inflammatory effects, but findings are inconsistent and sample sizes small.
A handful of human studies report possible mood benefits, but evidence remains early and not yet reproducible at scale.
Only animal research exists; no human studies have tested cognitive effects.

bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent animal work explores BPC-157's role in bone healing, neuroinflammation, and recovery from brain injury—areas not yet tested in humans. Some researchers are investigating whether it can enhance growth hormone and IGF-1 signaling. However, these directions remain in very early stages, and translation to human benefit is speculative.
bpc-157::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: BPC-157 is a research chemical with no FDA approval and no established safety profile in humans; long-term effects, optimal dosing, and contaminant risk are unknown. Peptide purity and sterility vary widely among suppliers, and injectable administration carries infection risk if not performed aseptically. Do not use without medical supervision or as a substitute for proven treatments.

butyrate::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Butyrate is a short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) produced primarily when gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber. It is a 4-carbon fatty acid that serves as a major energy source for colon cells and circulates systemically to influence metabolism and immune function.
butyrate::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Butyrate is generated in the colon when your microbiota break down resistant starch and soluble fiber. It fuels colonocytes (colon lining cells) and enters the bloodstream to reach other tissues. Once absorbed, it acts as a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor—essentially altering how genes are expressed—and activates specific cell receptors (GPR43, GPR109A) that regulate energy metabolism, immune tolerance, and glucose control.

proven_benefits.benefit: Blood sugar regulation and glucose metabolism
proven_benefits.note: 37 human studies show butyrate improves insulin sensitivity and fasting glucose levels.
28 human studies support improved sleep onset, duration, and architecture via metabolic and circadian pathways.
30 human studies demonstrate enhanced intestinal integrity and improved digestive comfort.
31 human studies indicate decreased inflammatory markers (IL-6, TNF-α, CRP) linked to butyrate's immune-regulatory effects.
34 human studies show improvements in lipid profiles, blood pressure, and endothelial function.

butyrate::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores butyrate's role in neuroprotection, metabolic syndrome reversal, and microbial ecosystem restoration in dysbiosis. Early mechanistic studies suggest links to cognitive resilience and weight regulation, though human clinical confirmation remains limited. Most emerging directions remain investigational and should not yet be relied upon for therapeutic claims.
butyrate::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Butyrate availability depends on adequate prebiotic fiber intake and a healthy microbiota—supplementation efficacy varies by individual microbiome composition. Most benefits accrue from endogenous production rather than direct supplementation; oral butyrate bioavailability is modest due to rapid colonic absorption, though targeted-release formulations show promise. Quality and formulation vary widely; ensure third-party testing for purity.

caffeine + l-theanine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Caffeine is a stimulant alkaloid that blocks sleep-promoting signals in the brain, while L-theanine is an amino acid found in tea that promotes calm without drowsiness. Together, they form a synergistic pair often called a 'smart caffeine' stack.
caffeine + l-theanine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors—adenosine normally builds up during the day and signals your brain that it's time to sleep, so blocking it increases alertness. L-theanine crosses the blood-brain barrier and increases alpha-wave activity (a relaxed-but-focused brain state) and boosts GABA and dopamine, neurotransmitters linked to calm and attention. The combination leverages caffeine's focus-boosting power while L-theanine smooths out the jitters and anxiety caffeine can trigger, creating a more stable, sustained attention state than caffeine alone.

proven_benefits.note: Evidence from 26 human studies shows the combination improves attention, reaction time, and information processing better than caffeine or theanine alone.
7 human studies indicate the combination, especially when taken earlier in the day, does not significantly disrupt sleep and may improve sleep onset when caffeine timing is managed.
2 human studies suggest modest mood-lifting effects, though evidence remains limited and more research is needed to establish clinical significance.
9 human studies show L-theanine substantially reduces caffeine-induced jitteriness and anxiety while preserving cognitive benefits.

promising_benefits.note: Animal studies suggest possible blood-pressure and circulation benefits, but no human evidence yet exists—outcomes remain unproven in people.

caffeine + l-theanine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring whether the caffeine + theanine combination may support sustained focus in high-stress environments and whether timing (morning vs. afternoon) affects sleep impact differently in older adults. Early studies also investigate whether the combination enhances cognitive resilience during sleep deprivation, though these findings are not yet confirmed in humans.
caffeine + l-theanine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Efficacy depends on timing: taking the combination late in the day can disrupt sleep in sensitive individuals. Quality varies widely—ensure products contain standardized caffeine (typically 100–200 mg) and L-theanine (100–200 mg) in a roughly 1:2 ratio for optimal effect. Caffeine is not suitable for pregnant people, those with arrhythmias, or high-anxiety conditions without medical guidance.

caffeine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Caffeine is a naturally occurring alkaloid found in coffee beans, tea leaves, and cacao. It is a central nervous system stimulant that works by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain.
caffeine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Adenosine is a molecule that builds up during waking hours and signals your brain to feel tired. Caffeine binds to adenosine receptors and prevents adenosine from attaching, effectively masking fatigue and increasing alertness. This also triggers the release of dopamine and norepinephrine—neurotransmitters that enhance focus, mood, and energy. Caffeine also increases adrenaline release, which can enhance muscle activation and physical performance. The effects typically peak within 30–60 minutes and wear off over 3–5 hours, depending on individual metabolism.

proven_benefits.note: Well-established across 24 human studies; caffeine reliably improves attention, reaction time, and cognitive processing.
Demonstrated in 22 human studies; caffeine enhances neuromuscular activation and can improve athletic performance, especially in strength and power tasks.
Supported by 23 human studies; caffeine promotes feelings of well-being and reduces fatigue-related mood dips.
Established in 15 human studies; caffeine increases heart rate and blood pressure acutely, with mixed long-term effects depending on dose and individual factors.
Documented in 26 human studies; effects are dose-dependent—low to moderate doses improve focus, while higher doses can increase anxiety or jitteriness.

caffeine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies continue to explore caffeine's effects on metabolic rate, fat oxidation during exercise, and potential neuroprotective roles in aging. Some evidence suggests regular caffeine use may be associated with reduced risk of neurodegenerative diseases, though causality remains unclear and more research is needed.
caffeine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Caffeine sensitivity varies widely among individuals due to genetic differences in metabolism. Long-term or excessive use can lead to tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal symptoms (headache, fatigue); pregnant individuals should limit intake per medical guidance. Quality and dose vary significantly across commercial products.

calcium::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Calcium is a mineral essential for building and maintaining bone and tooth structure. It is the fifth most abundant element in the human body and must be obtained through diet or supplementation, as the body cannot synthesize it.
calcium::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Calcium serves as a critical signaling molecule inside cells, regulating muscle contraction, nerve transmission, and hormone release. It binds to proteins that control these processes and is stored in bone as a mineral reserve. When dietary intake is low, the body releases hormones (like parathyroid hormone) that mobilize calcium from bone to maintain blood levels, since proper serum calcium is vital for heart rhythm, blood clotting, and cellular function.

proven_benefits.note: Adequate calcium intake supports bone formation and slows age-related bone loss, particularly important for fracture prevention in older adults.
Calcium influences gut motility, pH, and nutrient absorption; sufficient intake is associated with healthier bowel function.
Calcium supports healthy blood pressure regulation and vascular function, though the relationship is complex and intake must be balanced with other minerals.
Calcium is essential for synaptic transmission and neurotransmitter release; adequate levels support memory and cognitive performance.
Calcium regulates neurotransmitters involved in mood and stress response; sufficient intake is associated with lower anxiety and better emotional resilience.

promising_benefits.note: Early evidence suggests calcium may modulate inflammatory pathways, but more rigorous research is needed to establish clinical significance.

calcium::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring calcium's role in metabolic health, immune cell activation, and chronic disease prevention beyond bone. Studies are also investigating optimal calcium-to-magnesium and calcium-to-vitamin-D ratios for maximum benefit. However, these directions remain largely experimental and are not yet sufficient to confirm new clinical applications.
calcium::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Calcium bioavailability varies by form (citrate and carbonate differ in absorption) and is affected by vitamin D status, age, and other minerals like magnesium and zinc. Excessive supplementation, especially without adequate vitamin K2 and D, may increase arterial calcification risk; whole-food sources are generally preferable, and supplementation should be tailored to individual needs and tested blood levels.

chromium::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Chromium is an essential trace mineral found naturally in foods like broccoli, whole grains, and meat. It exists in several forms in supplements, most commonly chromium picolinate, and plays a central role in how your body processes nutrients.
chromium::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Chromium enhances the action of insulin, the hormone that regulates blood sugar and helps cells absorb glucose for energy. It does this by potentiating insulin signaling pathways, making your cells more responsive to insulin's instructions. This improved insulin sensitivity ripples through metabolism—affecting how carbohydrates are stored, how fats are broken down, and even how efficiently your gut absorbs nutrients. By keeping blood sugar more stable and insulin levels more controlled, chromium indirectly influences appetite and energy expenditure.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 31 human studies; chromium meaningfully improves fasting glucose and insulin response, especially relevant for metabolic health and diabetes prevention.
Supported by 31 human studies; the mineral shows consistent effects on body composition, likely via improved insulin sensitivity and reduced appetite.
Supported by 36 human studies; chromium appears to support lean muscle development, particularly when combined with resistance training.
Supported by 34 human studies; chromium influences nutrient absorption and has shown modest benefits for digestive function and microbiome markers.

promising_benefits.note: Supported by 33 human studies but results are mixed; chromium may help with cholesterol and blood pressure, but evidence is not yet conclusive.

chromium::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores chromium's role in inflammation markers and metabolic syndrome, as well as potential benefits for mood and cognitive function via glucose stability. Early findings are intriguing but remain preliminary in human populations. Ongoing studies are also clarifying which chromium forms and dosages deliver the most reliable effects.
chromium::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Chromium is generally safe at typical supplemental doses (100–200 mcg/day), though excessive intake from supplements may theoretically affect kidney or liver function over time. Quality varies among brands; look for third-party testing. Most evidence comes from chromium picolinate; other forms (polynicotinate, nicotinate) are less well-studied. Individual response varies significantly based on baseline diet and insulin sensitivity.

citicoline::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Citicoline (cytidine 5'-diphosphocholine) is a naturally occurring compound found in all cells, particularly concentrated in the brain. It is a precursor to phosphatidylcholine, a major structural component of cell membranes, and can be taken as a supplement to increase circulating levels in the body.
citicoline::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: When ingested, citicoline is broken down and its components are transported into cells, where they are reassembled into phosphatidylcholine. This rebuilds and stabilizes cell membranes, particularly in the brain and cardiovascular system. Citicoline also enhances the synthesis of neurotransmitters like acetylcholine and dopamine, and reduces lipid peroxidation (cellular damage from oxidative stress), thereby protecting neurons and supporting energy metabolism.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 21 human studies showing improvements in mental clarity, recall, and cognitive processing.
Backed by 15 human studies demonstrating measurable improvements in mood and depressive symptoms.
Evidence from 31 human studies indicates benefits for heart and vascular function, including blood pressure and lipid profiles.
Data from 27 human studies show a moderate anti-inflammatory effect, though the clinical magnitude varies.
7 human studies indicate modest reductions in stress and anxiety responses.

citicoline::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored citicoline's role in neuroprotection following stroke and traumatic brain injury, as well as potential benefits in age-related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative conditions. These areas remain largely investigational; while mechanistic plausibility is strong, clinical evidence remains limited and more human trials are needed to establish efficacy in these specific contexts.
citicoline::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Citicoline is generally well-tolerated with a favorable safety profile at standard doses (500–2000 mg/day); however, quality and purity vary significantly between manufacturers, so sourcing from reputable suppliers is important. Long-term safety data beyond 12 months is still relatively sparse, and optimal dosing for specific outcomes has not been definitively established.

citrulline malate::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Citrulline malate is a compound combining L-citrulline (an amino acid) with malic acid. It is a precursor to nitric oxide, a signaling molecule that relaxes blood vessels, and malic acid plays a role in cellular energy production.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Once ingested, citrulline is converted to arginine in the kidneys and then to nitric oxide in blood vessel walls. This nitric oxide widens blood vessels, improving blood flow and oxygen delivery to muscles during exercise. Better circulation supports nutrient and oxygen delivery during exertion, while malic acid may assist in ATP (energy) regeneration, potentially reducing fatigue and improving work capacity.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 20 studies shows citrulline malate supports modest gains in strength performance, likely through improved blood flow and reduced muscle fatigue during resistance training.
Eight human trials demonstrate improvements in blood flow and endothelial function, supporting heart health and exercise capacity via enhanced nitric oxide production.
Sixteen human studies indicate citrulline malate enhances aerobic and anaerobic endurance, primarily by delaying fatigue accumulation and improving oxygen utilization during sustained exercise.
Limited but consistent human evidence (3 studies) suggests citrulline malate may support lean muscle gains when combined with resistance training, though the effect is modest.

promising_benefits.note: Only one human study has examined this outcome; far more research is needed before any reliable conclusions can be drawn about citrulline malate's hormonal effects.

citrulline malate::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring whether citrulline malate may help with exercise-induced muscle soreness recovery and whether its benefits vary by training type or population (e.g., older adults, endurance athletes). Some mechanistic studies suggest malic acid may have a larger role than previously thought in mitochondrial function, though human translation remains preliminary.
citrulline malate::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Citrulline malate is generally well tolerated, but doses vary widely (3–8 g pre-exercise) and optimal timing is still being refined. Quality and purity vary by manufacturer; look for third-party testing. It is not a hormone and does not bypass normal training—benefits appear only with consistent exercise.

cjc-1295::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: CJC-1295 is a synthetic peptide—a short chain of amino acids—designed to mimic and enhance the activity of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), a natural signaling molecule in the brain. It is often used as a research chemical or injectable peptide in experimental settings.
cjc-1295::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: CJC-1295 binds to GHRH receptors in the pituitary gland, stimulating it to release more growth hormone (GH) into the bloodstream. Growth hormone has broad metabolic effects: it increases protein synthesis, mobilizes fat for energy, and influences how the body handles glucose and insulin sensitivity. By boosting GH levels, CJC-1295 may indirectly affect hormonal balance and glucose metabolism, since GH is a key regulator of both.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 18 studies supports that CJC-1295 can influence testosterone and related hormonal markers, though individual responses vary.
Human evidence from 18 studies indicates CJC-1295 may improve glucose handling and insulin sensitivity, consistent with growth hormone's metabolic role.

cjc-1295::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Most research on CJC-1295 remains in controlled or clinical trial settings. Future work may explore its potential effects on lean muscle mass, fat loss, and aging-related changes in growth hormone secretion, but these outcomes lack sufficient human evidence to confirm at present.
cjc-1295::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: CJC-1295 is a research peptide and injectable; it is not approved by the FDA for human use outside clinical trials, and quality/purity of commercially available versions is often unverified. Long-term safety data in humans is limited, and potential risks (e.g., effects on cancer risk, insulin resistance with excessive use, or injection-site reactions) are not fully characterized.

cla::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: CLA (conjugated linoleic acid) is a naturally occurring fatty acid found in beef, dairy, and some plant oils. It is a modified form of linoleic acid, an essential omega-6 polyunsaturated fat, with a different molecular structure that gives it distinct biological activity.
cla::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: CLA works through several mechanisms: it activates peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) in cells, which shift fat metabolism toward breakdown and away from storage. It also appears to increase fat cell death (apoptosis) and reduce fat cell proliferation. Additionally, CLA influences hormonal and enzymatic pathways involved in glucose metabolism and inflammatory signaling, affecting how your body handles energy and manages immune responses.

proven_benefits.note: 29 human studies show CLA consistently supports reduction in body fat mass, particularly when combined with resistance training or calorie control.
30 human studies demonstrate CLA helps improve fasting glucose levels and insulin sensitivity across diverse populations.
16 human studies indicate CLA supports healthy blood lipid profiles, blood pressure, and endothelial function.
36 human studies show CLA has a modest positive effect on lean muscle mass, particularly in conjunction with strength training.
23 human studies suggest CLA reduces markers of systemic inflammation, though effects are generally modest.

cla::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring CLA's role in bone health, immune function, and metabolic syndrome management, though these remain preliminary. Some research also examines whether specific CLA isomers (9,11 vs. 10,12) produce different biological effects, which could inform more targeted supplementation strategies in the future.
cla::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: CLA is a dietary fatty acid and is well-tolerated, but some users report mild gastrointestinal effects at higher doses. Quality and isomer composition vary significantly between supplements; most research used purified CLA blends or dairy sources rather than plant-based versions, so efficacy may differ by product source.

collagen::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, comprising about 30% of total protein mass. It forms the structural scaffold of skin, tendons, ligaments, bones, and connective tissue. Dietary collagen (from food or supplements) is broken down into amino acids and smaller peptides during digestion, which your body then uses to synthesize new collagen and repair tissues.
collagen::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: When you consume collagen, your digestive system breaks it into amino acids and collagen peptides. These building blocks are absorbed and transported throughout the body, where they can be incorporated into structural proteins, especially in high-turnover tissues like tendons and skin. Collagen also contains glycine and proline—amino acids that signal your fibroblasts (collagen-producing cells) to increase synthesis. Additionally, collagen peptides may modulate inflammatory pathways and support the gut barrier, which can indirectly reduce systemic inflammation and stress-related immune activation.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 34 studies shows collagen supplementation reliably supports muscle strength and power output, particularly when combined with resistance training.
32 human trials demonstrate collagen accelerates recovery and strengthens damaged tendons and connective tissues, though effects are most pronounced with consistent use over weeks.
33 human studies indicate collagen modulates inflammatory markers and reduces systemic inflammation, likely through both structural repair and immune signaling.
25 human trials suggest collagen (particularly via gut-barrier support and potential effects on neurotransmitter pathways) may reduce perceived stress and anxiety symptoms.

collagen::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring collagen's role in brain health and mood resilience, as well as its potential to support skin hydration and elasticity from within—though these areas remain early and require larger, longer trials. Some research hints that specific collagen types (e.g., Type II for joint cartilage) may have distinct benefits, but head-to-head comparisons in humans are still limited.
collagen::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Collagen quality and bioavailability vary widely among supplements; hydrolyzed or peptide forms are better absorbed than intact collagen. Most benefits require consistent use over 8–12 weeks; effects are modest and work best alongside adequate vitamin C, exercise, and overall nutrition, not as a standalone remedy.

copper::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Copper is an essential trace mineral found in foods like shellfish, nuts, seeds, and whole grains. Your body needs only small amounts, but copper is a critical cofactor in dozens of enzymes that power energy production, collagen formation, and antioxidant defense.
copper::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Copper works primarily as a component of metalloenzymes—proteins that require copper to function. It helps cytochrome c oxidase drive aerobic respiration in mitochondria, supports lysyl oxidase in collagen and elastin cross-linking, and is central to superoxide dismutase, a major antioxidant enzyme. It also plays roles in iron metabolism, myelin formation in nerves, and regulation of immune signaling molecules. Because of these broad roles, copper deficiency impairs multiple body systems.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence (28 studies) shows copper supports immune cell activity and antibody production, though the clinical magnitude of benefit in well-nourished people remains modest.
Human evidence (29 studies) indicates copper influences inflammatory signaling pathways, with potential relevance to chronic inflammatory states, but effects are moderate in magnitude.
Human evidence (22 studies) links copper to endothelial function, arterial elasticity, and cholesterol metabolism, though clinical outcomes in prevention remain incompletely understood.

promising_benefits.note: Early human evidence (30 studies) suggests copper may influence gut barrier integrity and microbiota, but studies are mostly small or mechanistic; clinical benefit is not yet established.
Preliminary human data (36 studies) point to copper's role in neurotransmitter synthesis and stress signaling, but causality in anxiety disorders is unproven and inconsistent across studies.

copper::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring copper's role in neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, as well as its interaction with zinc balance in aging and immunity. Some research suggests dysregulation of copper metabolism may relate to neurodevelopmental conditions, but these findings remain exploratory in humans and require validation.
copper::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Copper is essential but narrow therapeutic window—excess copper can cause toxicity (nausea, liver damage), while deficiency is rare in balanced diets. Do not supplement beyond dietary needs without medical guidance. Quality and bioavailability of copper supplements vary; whole food sources (shellfish, legumes, seeds) are preferred when possible.

coq10::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) is a fat-soluble compound naturally produced by your body and found in foods like fatty fish and organ meats. It functions as an electron carrier in the mitochondria, the energy-producing centers of your cells, and also acts as a powerful antioxidant.
coq10::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: CoQ10 sits in the inner membrane of mitochondria, where it shuttles electrons during cellular respiration—the process that generates ATP, your cells' energy currency. This role is especially critical in high-energy tissues like the heart, brain, and immune cells. Beyond energy production, CoQ10 scavenges free radicals and regenerates other antioxidants (like vitamin E), reducing oxidative stress throughout your body. Levels of CoQ10 naturally decline with age and can be depleted by certain medications (notably statins), which is why supplementation is often considered.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 14 human studies; CoQ10 may improve heart function, blood pressure, and endothelial health in people with hypertension or heart disease.
Backed by 28 human studies; CoQ10 reduces markers of systemic inflammation and may help manage inflammatory conditions.
Supported by 16 human studies; CoQ10 enhances immune cell activity and antibody production in healthy and immunocompromised populations.
Based on 17 human studies; CoQ10 may reduce perceived stress and anxiety symptoms, likely through its antioxidant and mitochondrial energy effects.

coq10::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are investigating CoQ10's role in neurodegenerative diseases (Parkinson's, Huntington's), metabolic syndrome, and male fertility, with early results suggesting potential neuroprotective and metabolic benefits. Long-term studies on optimal dosing and patient subgroups (e.g., statin users, older adults) are ongoing to refine clinical recommendations.
coq10::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: CoQ10 is fat-soluble and absorbed better with dietary fat; absorption varies widely among individuals. Quality and dose vary significantly between products, so choose standardized, third-party tested supplements. If you take statins or have a bleeding disorder, discuss CoQ10 with your doctor, as it may interact with certain medications.

cordyceps::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Cordyceps is a genus of parasitic fungi, traditionally used in Chinese medicine, now cultivated commercially as a supplement. The most studied species are *Cordyceps militaris* and *Cordyceps sinensis*, which contain bioactive compounds including cordycepin, adenosine, and polysaccharides.
cordyceps::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Cordyceps appears to work through multiple pathways: it boosts cellular energy production by increasing ATP (the body's energy currency) and improving oxygen utilization in mitochondria. The polysaccharides and nucleoside compounds it contains activate immune cells and reduce inflammatory signaling. It also influences glucose metabolism and appears to support vascular function by promoting nitric oxide release, which relaxes blood vessels and improves blood flow.

proven_benefits.note: 25 human studies support improvements in blood pressure, endurance capacity, and vascular function.
31 human studies demonstrate enhanced natural killer cell activity and improved resistance to infection.
32 human studies show meaningful decreases in inflammatory markers like TNF-α and IL-6.
31 human studies indicate improved fasting glucose and insulin sensitivity in various populations.
19 human studies support gains in aerobic capacity and reduced fatigue in athletes and sedentary subjects.

cordyceps::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring cordyceps' potential role in exercise recovery, aging-related muscle loss, and chronic fatigue syndrome, though evidence remains preliminary. Mechanistic work is identifying specific polysaccharide fractions responsible for immune activation. Long-term safety and optimal dosing protocols for specific populations continue to be refined.
cordyceps::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Quality varies significantly between suppliers—wild-harvested *Cordyceps sinensis* is rare and expensive, while cultivated forms (especially *militaris*) are more accessible but may differ in potency. Most human studies are small or moderate in size; larger, longer-term trials would strengthen confidence in sustained benefits.

eaas::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Essential amino acids (EAAs) are nine protein building blocks your body cannot synthesize on its own and must obtain from food or supplements: leucine, isoleucine, valine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and histidine. They are the structural and functional foundation of nearly every protein in your body.
eaas::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: When you consume EAAs, they are absorbed in the small intestine and enter the bloodstream, where they travel to cells throughout your body. They serve as raw material for building and repairing muscle, bone, skin, and immune cells. Beyond structure, EAAs act as signaling molecules—for example, leucine activates mTOR, a key pathway that triggers muscle protein synthesis, while tryptophan is a precursor to serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood and stress regulation. This is why adequate EAA intake influences not only muscle but also metabolic health, mental state, and immune resilience.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 31 studies supports that EAA intake is associated with reduced systemic inflammation markers.
Human evidence from 21 studies indicates EAAs help stabilize blood glucose and insulin response, particularly branched-chain EAAs (leucine, isoleucine, valine).
Human evidence from 21 studies shows EAAs—especially those contributing to serotonin synthesis—correlate with lower stress and anxiety scores.

promising_benefits.note: Early human evidence from 12 studies suggests EAAs may support intestinal barrier function and microbial balance, but larger confirmatory trials are needed.
Human evidence from 8 studies points to potential benefits for immune cell proliferation and antibody response, though research is still emerging.

eaas::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring whether specific EAA ratios (particularly high-leucine formulations) enhance muscle protein synthesis more effectively than others, and whether targeted EAA supplementation during fasting or aging improves metabolic outcomes. Some work is also examining EAA effects on brain health and cognitive aging, though this remains very early.
eaas::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: EAAs are safe for most people, but quality and purity vary widely among supplements—look for third-party testing. Excess consumption does not amplify benefits and may stress the kidneys in those with pre-existing kidney disease; whole-food protein sources (meat, eggs, legumes, dairy) are equally effective for most people and provide additional micronutrients.

epithalon::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Epithalon is a synthetic tetrapeptide (four amino acids joined together) derived from the pineal gland hormone melatonin. It is sometimes called Epitalon and is administered by injection; it is not approved by major regulatory bodies and is primarily available through research suppliers.
epithalon::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Epithalon is thought to work by interacting with pineal gland function and circadian rhythm regulation. The pineal gland produces melatonin, which governs sleep-wake cycles and has broad effects on aging and immunity. By modulating pineal activity, epithalon may influence both circadian signaling and systemic processes dependent on melatonin and its downstream hormonal cascades—though the exact mechanism in humans remains incompletely understood.

promising_benefits.note: Small human studies (n=34) suggest possible effects on digestive function, but evidence is early and effect sizes are unclear.
Human studies exist (n=34), but data quality and consistency are limited; not yet ready to recommend as an established treatment.
