Animal studies (n=6) hint at immune modulation, but no human evidence exists.
Only two animal studies; human hormonal effects are entirely unproven.

epithalon::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Most epithalon research has focused on circadian and pineal-mediated aging in animal models and small human cohorts. Recent work has explored stress-response and GI effects, but studies remain small and mechanistic details are sparse. Given its short history in humans, long-term safety and real-world efficacy remain largely unknown.
epithalon::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Epithalon is not FDA-approved and is sold primarily as a research chemical; quality, purity, and sterility are not guaranteed and vary widely between suppliers. As an injectable peptide, it carries infection risk if not handled properly. All claimed human benefits remain at a preliminary stage—do not use as a substitute for established medical treatments.

evening primrose oil::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Evening primrose oil is a plant oil extracted from the seeds of the evening primrose plant, rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids—particularly gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), an omega-6 fat. It is typically taken as a supplement in capsule form.
evening primrose oil::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: GLA is converted in the body into dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA), a precursor to anti-inflammatory signaling molecules called eicosanoids. These eicosanoids help regulate immune responses and reduce production of pro-inflammatory compounds. By shifting the balance toward these anti-inflammatory pathways, evening primrose oil can dampen excessive inflammation throughout the body, which has downstream effects on cardiovascular function and glucose regulation.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 30 human studies showing consistent reductions in inflammatory markers and symptoms in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis.
39 human studies indicate benefits for lipid profiles and blood pressure, likely via anti-inflammatory and vascular effects.
25 human studies show modest improvements in fasting glucose and insulin sensitivity in people with diabetes or metabolic dysfunction.

promising_benefits.note: Only 2 human studies available; results are suggestive but too limited to draw firm conclusions about hormonal effects.
A single human study reported benefit; far more research is needed to establish whether evening primrose oil reliably affects mood or stress.

evening primrose oil::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored evening primrose oil's potential in autoimmune conditions beyond rheumatoid arthritis, as well as its role in hormone-sensitive skin conditions. Some studies are investigating whether GLA may support immune regulation in allergic and inflammatory skin disorders. However, these investigations remain early, and clinical significance has not yet been firmly established.
evening primrose oil::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Evening primrose oil is generally well-tolerated, though high doses may cause mild gastrointestinal upset or interact with blood-thinning medications; consult a healthcare provider if taking anticoagulants. Quality and GLA content vary between supplements; look for third-party testing to ensure consistency.

fenugreek::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Fenugreek is a legume plant (Trigonella foenum-graecum) native to South Asia, with seeds that contain bioactive compounds including alkaloids, saponins, and fiber. It has been used in traditional medicine and cuisine for centuries, and is now studied for metabolic and hormonal effects.
fenugreek::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Fenugreek seeds work through multiple pathways: their soluble fiber slows glucose absorption in the gut, reducing blood sugar spikes; saponins and alkaloids may enhance insulin sensitivity and secretion; polyphenols reduce oxidative stress and inflammatory markers; and certain compounds appear to influence hormone signaling, particularly affecting testosterone and other androgens. The seed's high fiber content also supports cardiovascular health by improving cholesterol profiles.

proven_benefits.note: 28 human studies show fenugreek reduces fasting glucose and improves glycemic control in both diabetic and non-diabetic populations.
14 human studies demonstrate improvements in cholesterol levels, triglycerides, and other cardiovascular risk markers.
28 human studies document decreases in inflammatory markers like C-reactive protein and inflammatory cytokines.
22 human studies show fenugreek positively influences testosterone levels and sexual/reproductive function in men.

promising_benefits.note: 19 human studies suggest potential cognitive benefits, but evidence remains mixed and inconsistent; further research is needed to establish clinical relevance.

fenugreek::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring fenugreek's role in weight management, muscle retention, and lactation in postpartum women, though these areas remain early-stage. Some research also investigates its effects on gut microbiota and metabolic syndrome as a whole. These directions are promising but require larger, well-designed trials before clinical recommendations can be made.
fenugreek::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Fenugreek is generally well-tolerated but may cause gastrointestinal upset in some users; those with legume allergies should avoid it. Quality varies by supplier—choose standardized extracts for consistency. Pregnant women should consult a healthcare provider before use, and it may interact with blood-thinning or diabetes medications.

fisetin::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Fisetin is a flavonoid—a plant compound found in strawberries, apples, onions, and other fruits and vegetables. It belongs to the polyphenol family, molecules known for their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.
fisetin::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Fisetin works primarily by neutralizing free radicals (unstable molecules that damage cells) and reducing inflammatory signaling pathways in the body. It activates cellular stress-response systems, particularly sirtuins and AMPK, which are linked to cellular repair and longevity processes. These mechanisms may help protect blood vessels, support brain function, and promote cellular resilience—though the full picture of how these lab effects translate to whole-body benefit in humans remains incomplete.

proven_benefits.note: Studies in humans show fisetin may support healthy blood pressure, endothelial function, and lipid profiles, though large randomized trials are still needed.
Human research suggests fisetin may support memory, processing speed, and overall mental clarity, though effect sizes vary and optimal dosing is not fully established.

promising_benefits.note: Animal studies show fisetin suppresses inflammatory markers, but human trials have not yet confirmed clinical benefit.
Very limited animal research suggests potential anxiolytic effects; human evidence is essentially absent.
Only rodent studies exist; no human data supports claims about muscle function or athletic performance.

fisetin::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored fisetin's role in cellular senescence (aging) and its potential as a senolytic—an agent that clears senescent cells. Studies in mice and cell cultures suggest promise, but human trials are in very early stages. Researchers are also investigating whether fisetin enhances the effects of other longevity-focused compounds, though these synergies remain theoretical.
fisetin::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Fisetin is a food-derived compound with a reasonable safety profile, but most human studies use supplemental doses higher than typical dietary intake; long-term safety at such levels is not fully characterized. Bioavailability varies widely depending on formulation, and quality/purity of commercial supplements can differ significantly—look for third-party testing.

fish oil::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Fish oil is a fat extracted from fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) that is rich in omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, primarily EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) and DHA (docosahexaenoic acid). These are essential fats your body cannot make on its own and must obtain from diet or supplements.
fish oil::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: EPA and DHA integrate into cell membranes throughout your body, where they influence cell signaling, reduce production of inflammatory molecules, and support neurotransmitter function. In the brain, DHA is a major structural component that helps maintain neural connections and may stabilize serotonin and dopamine pathways. In the cardiovascular system, these fats help regulate blood vessel function, reduce triglycerides, and lower inflammatory markers that contribute to arterial damage. In the gut, omega-3s promote beneficial bacteria growth and strengthen the intestinal barrier.

proven_benefits.note: Substantial human evidence (28 studies) shows fish oil can support mood regulation and reduce depressive symptoms, likely through effects on brain serotonin and inflammation.
Well-supported by human research (28 studies) demonstrating measurable reductions in systemic inflammatory markers.
Consistent human evidence (22 studies) shows benefits for heart health markers including blood pressure, triglycerides, and arterial function.
Supported by human studies (29 studies) indicating improvements in gut barrier function and beneficial changes to bacterial composition.
Moderate human evidence (26 studies) suggests fish oil can help reduce anxiety and support stress resilience, though effects vary by individual.

fish oil::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent research is exploring whether omega-3s may support cognitive aging and whether specific EPA-to-DHA ratios optimize different outcomes (mood vs. cardiovascular). Some studies are investigating fish oil's role in autoimmune conditions and metabolic health, though these remain early-stage investigations.
fish oil::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Fish oil supplements vary widely in EPA/DHA content and purity; third-party testing is advisable. High doses may increase bleeding risk in those on anticoagulants, and some users report fish-flavored aftertaste or mild gastrointestinal upset. Quality sources and consistent dosing matter for reliable benefits.

flaxseed::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Flaxseed is the small, nutrient-dense seed of the flax plant (Linum usitatissimum), rich in alpha-linolenic acid (an omega-3 fatty acid), soluble fiber, and polyphenolic compounds called lignans. It is consumed whole, ground, or as an oil extract.
flaxseed::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Flaxseed's omega-3 content and lignans work to reduce inflammatory signaling pathways in the body, while its high soluble fiber content slows glucose absorption and supports beneficial gut bacteria. The combination helps stabilize blood sugar levels, reduce systemic inflammation, and improve cholesterol and triglyceride profiles—all of which support heart health. The same anti-inflammatory and fiber-based mechanisms may also help calm nervous system activation related to stress and anxiety.

proven_benefits.note: 17 human studies show flaxseed improves cholesterol profiles, blood pressure, and arterial function.
31 human studies demonstrate consistent reductions in inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6) across diverse populations.
32 human studies show flaxseed improves fasting glucose, insulin sensitivity, and glycemic response to meals.
37 human studies indicate benefits for bowel regularity, microbial diversity, and digestive comfort, though effects vary by individual.
5 human studies suggest modest improvements in perceived stress and anxiety symptoms, though the evidence base is smaller.

flaxseed::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring flaxseed's role in bone health, hormonal balance (particularly in women), and cognitive function, though these areas remain preliminary. Some research also investigates whether the lignan content specifically—rather than the omega-3 alone—drives anti-inflammatory and metabolic benefits, a distinction that could refine recommendations. More mechanistic work is underway to clarify which populations benefit most and optimal dosing.
flaxseed::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Flaxseed is generally well-tolerated at typical dietary doses (1–2 tablespoons daily), but excess intake may cause digestive upset; ensure adequate hydration, especially with ground flaxseed. Quality varies by supplier; whole seeds store longer than ground or oil. People on blood-thinning medications should check with their provider, as large amounts of flaxseed may have mild anticoagulant effects. The evidence grades above reflect human studies, but individual responses to flaxseed depend on baseline diet, genetics, and health status.

folate::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Folate is a B vitamin (B9) that occurs naturally in foods like leafy greens, legumes, and eggs. Your body uses it to make and repair DNA, and to produce neurotransmitters—the chemical messengers in your brain.
folate::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Folate acts as a methyl donor, meaning it helps transfer chemical groups that regulate gene expression and neurotransmitter synthesis throughout your body. It is especially important for converting homocysteine (an amino acid byproduct) into methionine, keeping homocysteine levels in a healthy range. Low folate disrupts this cycle, which can impair mood regulation, stress resilience, and inflammatory control. It also supports gut barrier function and the microbial environment your digestive system depends on.

proven_benefits.note: 27 human studies show folate supports stress resilience and anxiety symptoms, likely through its role in neurotransmitter and methyl-group metabolism.
16 human studies demonstrate folate's association with improved mood and reduced depressive symptoms, particularly when deficiency is corrected.
25 human studies indicate folate supports gut barrier integrity and healthy digestive function.
29 human studies show folate helps regulate inflammatory markers, partly by lowering homocysteine levels.

promising_benefits.note: 17 human studies suggest folate may support cardiovascular function, but evidence is not yet conclusive and further research is needed.

folate::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring folate's role in epigenetic regulation—how it influences which genes are 'switched on or off'—which may have implications for long-term brain health and aging. Some studies are also investigating whether optimal folate status enhances the effectiveness of mental-health interventions. These directions are early and require more human data.
folate::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Folate is a safe, water-soluble vitamin with no established toxicity at high doses from food or standard supplementation. However, people taking certain medications (like methotrexate) or with specific genetic variations in folate metabolism should consult a healthcare provider; synthetic folic acid may not be ideal for everyone, and methylfolate or L-5-MTHF are alternative forms worth discussing with your doctor.

garlic extract::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Garlic extract is a concentrated preparation derived from garlic bulbs (Allium sativum), containing sulfur-containing compounds like allicin, ajoene, and diallyl disulfide as active constituents. These compounds are responsible for garlic's pungent smell and much of its biological activity.
garlic extract::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Garlic extract works through multiple pathways in the body. Its sulfur compounds act as antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents, helping neutralize free radicals and dampen inflammatory signaling. They also support healthy blood vessel function by promoting nitric oxide production, which improves blood flow and helps regulate blood pressure. Additionally, garlic compounds may enhance insulin sensitivity and improve how cells handle glucose, supporting metabolic health.

proven_benefits.note: Well-established human evidence (19 studies) shows garlic extract supports healthy blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and overall heart function.
Robust human evidence (25 studies) demonstrates garlic's ability to reduce inflammatory markers and support immune balance.
Substantial human data (29 studies) shows garlic extract helps improve fasting glucose levels and insulin sensitivity.
Human evidence (25 studies) supports benefits for memory and mental clarity, though effects are more modest than cardiovascular benefits.

promising_benefits.note: Very early-stage research (animal-only, 1 study); human evidence is lacking, so this potential benefit remains unproven.

garlic extract::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent investigations are exploring garlic extract's potential role in supporting brain health as we age and its ability to modulate gut microbiota, which may have downstream immune and metabolic effects. Some researchers are also examining whether garlic compounds may support athletic performance and recovery, though these remain very early findings. Human studies in these areas are still limited.
garlic extract::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Garlic extract is generally well-tolerated, though high doses may cause digestive upset or interact with blood-thinning medications; consult a healthcare provider if taking anticoagulants. Quality and allicin content vary widely between commercial supplements, so standardized extracts are preferable for consistent results.

ghk-cu::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring copper-binding tripeptide (glycine-histidine-lysine complexed with copper) found in human plasma, saliva, and urine. It is often synthesized or extracted for research and therapeutic investigation.
ghk-cu::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: GHK-Cu acts as a signaling molecule that binds to specific cell-surface receptors and influences gene expression related to collagen synthesis, tissue remodeling, and immune regulation. Copper is essential to its function, as it facilitates enzymatic activity and antioxidant processes. The peptide appears to modulate growth factors and reduce inflammatory signaling pathways in various cell types. It may also support cellular repair and wound healing responses, though the full cascade of effects in living humans remains incompletely understood.

promising_benefits.note: Animal studies suggest potential for collagen remodeling and wound repair; human evidence is absent.
A modest human evidence base (20 studies) hints at anti-inflammatory effects, but results are not yet definitive or consistently replicated.
Animal models show some neuroprotective promise; no human studies confirm cognitive benefits.
Human studies (29 total) suggest possible anxiolytic effects, but evidence is early and heterogeneous in quality.
Limited human data (5 studies) raises questions about vascular function; too few trials to establish safety or efficacy.

ghk-cu::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored GHK-Cu's role in skin aging, fibrosis reversal, and neuroinflammation, with particular interest in its ability to reprogram gene expression toward tissue regeneration. Early mechanistic studies hint at broad potential across aging and degenerative conditions. However, these directions remain largely preclinical or confined to small, preliminary human trials.
ghk-cu::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: GHK-Cu is often marketed as a research peptide and is not approved by the FDA for human use; purity, stability, and sterility of commercial sources are highly variable and largely unregulated. The safety profile in humans is poorly established, particularly at higher doses or with repeated administration, and long-term effects are unknown.

ginger::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Ginger is a rhizome (underground stem) from the flowering plant Zingiber officinale, native to Southeast Asia. It contains bioactive compounds called gingerols and shogaols, which are responsible for its pungent flavor and biological activity.
ginger::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Ginger's active compounds work through multiple mechanisms: they inhibit inflammatory signaling pathways (particularly NF-κB and COX enzymes), reduce prostaglandin production, and enhance gastric motility and digestive enzyme secretion. These actions reduce inflammation systemically, improve stomach function and nutrient absorption, and modulate glucose metabolism. Ginger also appears to influence hormone production and cardiovascular function through antioxidant activity and effects on blood vessel function.

proven_benefits.note: Supported by 33 human studies; ginger consistently lowers inflammatory markers and is well-established for managing inflammatory conditions.
Backed by 34 human studies; ginger accelerates gastric emptying, reduces nausea, and improves overall digestive comfort.
Supported by 33 human studies; ginger improves insulin sensitivity and helps maintain healthy glucose levels.
Based on 20 human studies; ginger may improve blood pressure, cholesterol profiles, and blood flow, though more research is ongoing.
Based on 31 human studies; ginger may modestly enhance testosterone levels and hormonal balance in certain populations, though effects are generally modest.

ginger::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring ginger's potential neuroprotective effects, its role in cognitive function, and its synergy with other anti-inflammatory compounds. Early work also suggests possible benefits for certain types of pain and migraine prevention, though these remain areas requiring further human evidence.
ginger::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Ginger is generally safe and well-tolerated, but high doses may cause mild gastrointestinal upset or interact with blood thinners; pregnant women should consult a healthcare provider. Quality varies significantly among commercial products—standardized extracts or whole rhizome tend to be more reliable than uncontrolled supplements.

ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Ginkgo biloba is an extract from leaves of the ginkgo tree, one of the oldest living tree species. It contains a complex mix of flavonoids and terpenoids—plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.
ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Ginkgo works through multiple pathways: its flavonoids neutralize free radicals that damage cells and blood vessels, while terpenoids improve blood flow and reduce inflammation throughout the body. It also modulates neurotransmitter activity and protects nerve cells from oxidative stress. This multi-target action affects both brain function (cognition, mood) and cardiovascular health, which in turn can reduce stress and anxiety.

proven_benefits.note: Robust human evidence (29 studies) shows ginkgo improves cognitive function, processing speed, and memory performance, particularly in aging populations.
Strong human evidence (19 studies) demonstrates improved blood flow, reduced clotting risk, and better vascular function.
Solid human evidence (20 studies) indicates ginkgo has mood-lifting effects and may reduce depressive symptoms, possibly through antioxidant neuroprotection.
Moderate human evidence (28 studies) shows ginkgo reduces systemic inflammatory markers, supporting its broader health effects.
Moderate human evidence (22 studies) suggests ginkgo reduces anxiety and perceived stress, likely via improved blood flow and neuroprotection.

ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring ginkgo's potential in age-related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative conditions, as well as its role in reducing tinnitus and improving sexual function. While early findings are encouraging, these applications remain under investigation and are not yet standard clinical recommendations.
ginkgo biloba::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Ginkgo can interact with blood thinners (warfarin, aspirin) and may increase bleeding risk; avoid or use cautiously if on anticoagulants. Extract quality and standardization vary widely between products; look for standardized extracts (typically 24% flavonoids, 6% terpenoids) for consistency. Long-term safety is generally good, but mild side effects (headache, stomach upset, allergic reactions) occur in some users.

ginseng::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Ginseng is a root from plants in the Panax genus, traditionally used in Asian medicine for over 2,000 years. It contains active compounds called ginsenosides, which are thought to drive most of its biological effects.
ginseng::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Ginsenosides appear to work through multiple pathways: they modulate the nervous system's stress response (via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis), improve blood vessel function and blood flow, dampen excessive immune inflammatory signals, and influence neurotransmitter activity related to mood and cognition. These actions affect energy production, vascular health, and how the body handles physical and mental stressors.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 20+ studies supports benefits for blood pressure, blood vessel function, and overall cardiovascular outcomes.
Moderate human evidence (30 studies) indicates ginseng can lower inflammatory markers, though effects are modest in many trials.
Moderate human evidence (34 studies) shows ginseng may reduce perceived stress and anxiety symptoms, likely through nervous system modulation.
Moderate human evidence (25 studies) suggests ginseng may improve mood and depressive symptoms, particularly when combined with other treatments.
Moderate human evidence (30 studies) indicates ginseng may enhance certain immune markers and reduce infection risk, though effects vary by type and dose.

ginseng::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work explores ginseng's potential role in cognitive aging, athletic endurance, and blood sugar regulation, but these findings remain preliminary and mostly limited to smaller studies or animal models. More large, well-controlled human trials are needed to clarify benefits in these areas.
ginseng::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Quality and ginsenoside content vary widely between commercial products; standardized extracts (4–7% ginsenosides) are preferred for consistency. Ginseng may interact with blood thinners, stimulants, and diabetes medications, and some people report sleep disruption if taken late in the day.

glucosamine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Glucosamine is a naturally occurring amino sugar found in cartilage, bone, and connective tissue. glucosamine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Glucosamine serves as a building block for glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans—the key structural molecules in cartilage and connective tissue. When ingested, it is absorbed and may accumulate in joint cartilage, where it supports the synthesis and repair of the extracellular matrix. Additionally, glucosamine appears to modulate inflammatory signaling pathways and influence gut barrier function, which may explain its broader systemic effects on inflammation and digestive health.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 29 studies suggests glucosamine may help improve fasting glucose levels and insulin sensitivity, though effects are modest and results are mixed across trials.
30 human studies indicate glucosamine can reduce markers of systemic inflammation and may support joint-specific inflammatory control, with consistent but moderate effect sizes.
36 human studies show glucosamine may strengthen the intestinal barrier, support healthy gut microbiota, and reduce digestive inflammation, though individual responses vary.

glucosamine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring glucosamine's role in metabolic health beyond blood sugar—including effects on lipid profiles and weight management—as well as its potential in supporting bone density and reducing cartilage degradation in aging populations. A few emerging trials are also investigating combination formulas pairing glucosamine with other compounds like chondroitin or collagen peptides, though these combination studies remain early-stage.
glucosamine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Glucosamine is generally well-tolerated, though some users report mild gastrointestinal symptoms; quality and bioavailability vary significantly between brands and formulations (sulfate vs. hydrochloride), which may explain variability in study outcomes. Long-term safety in very high doses and in specific populations (e.g., pregnant women, those with shellfish allergies) remains incompletely characterized.

glutamine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Glutamine is a non-essential amino acid—one of the 20 building blocks of protein—that your body produces naturally but can also obtain from food (especially meat, dairy, and legumes) or supplements. It is the most abundant free amino acid in your bloodstream and plays central roles in energy metabolism, immune function, and gut barrier integrity.
glutamine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Glutamine serves as a primary fuel source for rapidly dividing cells, particularly immune cells (white blood cells) and intestinal epithelial cells that line your gut. It also acts as a precursor for glutathione, a potent antioxidant, and supports the synthesis of other amino acids and nucleotides needed for protein and DNA synthesis. During physical stress, illness, or intense exercise, your body's glutamine demand exceeds its natural production, which is why supplementation may be beneficial during these periods.

proven_benefits.note: Multiple human studies support glutamine's role in maintaining gut barrier function and digestive integrity, particularly in clinical and high-stress populations.
Evidence from 21 human studies shows glutamine supports immune cell production and activity, especially relevant during intense training or illness.
Human studies indicate glutamine may help modulate inflammatory markers and support recovery from inflammatory stress.
Research suggests glutamine supports healthy glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity in human populations.

promising_benefits.note: 31 human studies exist, but evidence remains mixed and inconclusive; glutamine may influence neurotransmitter pathways relevant to mood, but effects are not yet reliably established.

glutamine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work is exploring glutamine's potential role in metabolic recovery after critical illness, its effects on microbiome composition, and possible applications in managing intestinal permeability in autoimmune conditions. However, these areas remain early-stage and require further investigation to draw clinical conclusions.
glutamine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Glutamine is generally well-tolerated, but quality and purity vary between supplement brands—look for third-party testing. People with certain kidney or liver conditions should consult a healthcare provider before supplementing. The evidence, while moderate, does not mean glutamine is a cure or replacement for medical treatment.

glycine::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Glycine is the smallest and simplest amino acid, a basic building block of protein found throughout the body. It makes up roughly one-third of collagen, the main structural protein in skin, tendons, and bone, and also functions as a neurotransmitter in the central nervous system.
glycine::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Glycine works through multiple pathways. In collagen and connective tissue, it provides structural support and is essential for cross-linking and strength. In the nervous system, glycine acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter, helping to calm neural activity and promote relaxation. It also participates in glutathione synthesis (a major antioxidant), reduces inflammatory signaling, and influences metabolic processes including glucose regulation. Its calming effect on the nervous system appears to be a key mechanism underlying its effects on sleep and stress response.

proven_benefits.note: Evidence supports glycine's role in dampening inflammatory markers and immune activation.
Glycine's inhibitory neurotransmitter activity correlates with reduced anxiety and improved stress resilience in human trials.
As a collagen precursor, glycine supports structural repair and recovery in connective tissue.
Glycine promotes deeper, more restorative sleep and faster sleep onset, likely through central nervous system relaxation.
Glycine influences glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity, with potential benefits for metabolic control.

glycine::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent research is exploring glycine's role in circadian rhythm regulation, mitochondrial function, and long-term metabolic health. Some studies suggest potential benefits in cognitive aging and neuroprotection, though these remain preliminary and require larger human trials. The compound's simplicity and multiple biological roles make it a continued focus for understanding how amino acid metabolism intersects with chronic disease prevention.
glycine::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: Glycine is a common dietary amino acid found in protein-rich foods and is generally well-tolerated at supplemental doses; however, very high intakes are not well-studied long-term. Quality varies by supplier, so sourcing from reputable manufacturers is important. Most evidence is moderate rather than strong, meaning clinical effect sizes are real but modest, and individual responses vary.

hmb::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: HMB (β-hydroxy β-methylbutyrate) is a metabolite of the branched-chain amino acid leucine, naturally produced in small amounts when your body breaks down protein. It is available as a supplement, typically in calcium or free-acid forms, to boost levels beyond what diet alone provides.
hmb::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: HMB works primarily by reducing muscle protein breakdown during and after exercise, a process called proteolysis. It activates mTOR signaling, a key pathway that promotes muscle protein synthesis and growth. By tilting the balance toward building muscle rather than breaking it down, HMB helps preserve and build lean mass during training and recovery, and may improve how efficiently your muscles generate force and sustain effort.

22 human studies demonstrate HMB increases lean muscle mass and supports hypertrophy in trained and untrained individuals.
25 human studies indicate HMB enhances endurance capacity and reduces fatigue accumulation during sustained effort.
30 human studies support improvements in aerobic markers and cardiovascular performance.
30 human studies suggest potential cognitive benefits, though the effect size and real-world relevance remain moderate.

hmb::clarity-engine-v2.emerging_research: Recent work has explored HMB's role in aging populations, with early findings suggesting it may help preserve muscle and function in older adults—particularly relevant given age-related muscle loss. Some studies are also investigating whether HMB could support recovery from injury or illness, though robust clinical evidence in these areas is still developing.
hmb::clarity-engine-v2.caveats: HMB is generally well-tolerated, though most studies involve relatively short intervention periods; long-term safety profiles in special populations remain understudied. Supplement quality varies by manufacturer, so third-party testing is recommended. Effects are most pronounced when combined with structured exercise and adequate protein intake; HMB alone is not a substitute for training.

holy basil::clarity-engine-v2.what_it_is: Holy basil (Ocimum sanctum), also called tulsi, is a perennial herb native to India with a long history in Ayurvedic medicine. holy basil::clarity-engine-v2.how_it_works: Holy basil appears to work through multiple pathways. It may reduce cortisol and other stress hormones, helping the body manage the physiological effects of anxiety. The herb contains polyphenols that act as antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents, potentially dampening inflammatory signaling in the body. It may also improve insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism through effects on cellular enzymes and signaling pathways, while supporting cardiovascular function through improvements in blood pressure and lipid profiles—though this last mechanism is less well characterized in humans.
